claim: p53 is the best-known tumor suppressor.
source: The transcription factor p53 is the best-known tumor suppressor, but its sibling p63 is a master regulator of epidermis development and a key oncogenic driver in squamous cell carcinomas (SCC).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about p53's role as a tumor suppressor.

claim: p63 is a master regulator of epidermis development.
source: The transcription factor p53 is the best-known tumor suppressor, but its sibling p63 is a master regulator of epidermis development and a key oncogenic driver in squamous cell carcinomas (SCC).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mills et al., 1999 and Yang et al., 1999 in the Introduction section.

claim: p63 is a key oncogenic driver in squamous cell carcinomas (SCC).
source: The transcription factor p53 is the best-known tumor suppressor, but its sibling p63 is a master regulator of epidermis development and a key oncogenic driver in squamous cell carcinomas (SCC).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2018 and Gatti et al., 2019.

claim: p63 is overexpressed or amplified in SCCs.
source: its phylogenetically ancient sibling p63 (ΔNp63) governs epidermis development (Mills et al., 1999; Yang et al., 1999) and is an oncogenic driver of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2018; Gatti et al., 2019) that is overexpressed or amplified in SCCs, which depend on its expression (Ramsey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ramsey et al., 2013.

claim: SCCs depend on p63 expression.
source: its phylogenetically ancient sibling p63 (ΔNp63) governs epidermis development (Mills et al., 1999; Yang et al., 1999) and is an oncogenic driver of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2018; Gatti et al., 2019) that is overexpressed or amplified in SCCs, which depend on its expression (Ramsey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ramsey et al., 2013.

claim: p63, p53, and p73 form the p53 transcription factor family.
source: Together with p73, p63, and p53 form the p53 transcription factor (TF) family that shares a highly conserved DNA binding domain (DBD) through which they bind to very similar DNA recognition motifs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the p53 family of transcription factors.

claim: The p53 family shares a highly conserved DNA binding domain (DBD).
source: Together with p73, p63, and p53 form the p53 transcription factor (TF) family that shares a highly conserved DNA binding domain (DBD) through which they bind to very similar DNA recognition motifs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structural similarity of p53 family members.

claim: p53 family members bind to very similar DNA recognition motifs.
source: Together with p73, p63, and p53 form the p53 transcription factor (TF) family that shares a highly conserved DNA binding domain (DBD) through which they bind to very similar DNA recognition motifs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the DNA binding properties of p53 family members.

claim: The TP53 and TP63 genes encode for two major isoform groups controlled by distinct promoters.
source: The TP53 and TP63 genes encode for two major isoform groups that are controlled by distinct promoters leading to transcripts differing in their N-terminus (Murray-Zmijewski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Murray-Zmijewski et al., 2006.

claim: p53α is ubiquitously expressed.
source: In the case of TP53, the longest isoform, p53α, is ubiquitously expressed while the alternative intronic promoter has little activity across virtually all tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p53 isoform expression patterns.

claim: The alternative intronic promoter of TP53 has little activity across virtually all tissues.
source: In the case of TP53, the longest isoform, p53α, is ubiquitously expressed while the alternative intronic promoter has little activity across virtually all tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TP53 promoter activity.

claim: The usage of the two TP63 promoters is highly cell type-dependent.
source: Conversely, the usage of the two TP63 promoters is highly cell type-dependent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TP63 promoter usage.

claim: TAp63 is predominantly expressed in germ cells.
source: For instance, the long isoform TAp63 is predominantly expressed in germ cells, while the smaller transcript, ΔNp63, is most copious in stratifying epithelia (Sethi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sethi et al., 2015.

claim: ΔNp63 is most copious in stratifying epithelia.
source: For instance, the long isoform TAp63 is predominantly expressed in germ cells, while the smaller transcript, ΔNp63, is most copious in stratifying epithelia (Sethi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sethi et al., 2015.

claim: Alternative splicing leads to α, β, and γ protein isoforms that differ in their C-terminus.
source: Similar to p53, alternative splicing leads to α, β, and γ protein isoforms that differ in their C-terminus (Murray-Zmijewski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Murray-Zmijewski et al., 2006.

claim: ΔNp63 lacks the canonical N-terminal transactivation domain (TAD).
source: While both TAp63 and ΔNp63 may bind to DNA through a specific binding domain, ΔNp63 lacks the canonical N-terminal transactivation domain (TAD) (Yang et al., 1998) and has long been thought to be a dominant-negative regulator of other p53 family members or its own isoforms (Gebel et al., 2016; Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 1998.

claim: ΔNp63 has long been thought to be a dominant-negative regulator of other p53 family members or its own isoforms.
source: While both TAp63 and ΔNp63 may bind to DNA through a specific binding domain, ΔNp63 lacks the canonical N-terminal transactivation domain (TAD) (Yang et al., 1998) and has long been thought to be a dominant-negative regulator of other p53 family members or its own isoforms (Gebel et al., 2016; Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gebel et al., 2016 and Yang et al., 1998.

claim: ΔNp63 has been shown to harbor alternative TADs that endow transactivation activity.
source: However, ΔNp63 has also been shown to harbor alternative TADs, that endow transactivation activity (Helton et al., 2006; King et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Helton et al., 2006, King et al., 2003, and Yang et al., 2006.

claim: Many ΔNp63-binding sites are associated with enhancer regions.
source: Notably, many ΔNp63-binding sites are associated with enhancer regions, where ΔNp63 has been proposed to 'bookmark' genes that are expressed in stratifying epithelia (Karsli Uzunbas et al., 2019; Kouwenhoven et al., 2015a; Lin-Shiao et al., 2019; Qu et al., 2018; Somerville et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: ΔNp63 has been proposed to 'bookmark' genes that are expressed in stratifying epithelia.
source: Notably, many ΔNp63-binding sites are associated with enhancer regions, where ΔNp63 has been proposed to 'bookmark' genes that are expressed in stratifying epithelia (Karsli Uzunbas et al., 2019; Kouwenhoven et al., 2015a; Lin-Shiao et al., 2019; Qu et al., 2018; Somerville et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: All three p53 family members have been shown to bind to substantial sets of unique target genes.
source: The p53 TF family shares many binding sites, but all three family members have been shown to bind to substantial sets of unique target genes (Lin et al., 2009; McDade et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2009 and McDade et al., 2014.

claim: There are differences in the DBDs of p53 family members regarding thermostability and hydrophobic potentials.
source: Indeed, there are differences in the DBDs, for example regarding thermostability, hydrophobic potentials (Enthart et al., 2016), zinc-coordination (Lokshin et al., 2007), and redox sensitivity (Tichý et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Enthart et al., 2016.

claim: There are differences in the DBDs of p53 family members regarding zinc-coordination.
source: Indeed, there are differences in the DBDs, for example regarding thermostability, hydrophobic potentials (Enthart et al., 2016), zinc-coordination (Lokshin et al., 2007), and redox sensitivity (Tichý et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lokshin et al., 2007.

claim: There are differences in the DBDs of p53 family members regarding redox sensitivity.
source: Indeed, there are differences in the DBDs, for example regarding thermostability, hydrophobic potentials (Enthart et al., 2016), zinc-coordination (Lokshin et al., 2007), and redox sensitivity (Tichý et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tichý et al., 2013.

claim: The different C-terminal domains (CTD) of p53 family members may affect their DNA binding specificity.
source: In addition, the different C-terminal domains (CTD) of p53 family members may also affect their DNA binding specificity (Sauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sauer et al., 2008.

claim: p53 binds to a canonical 20 bp response element (RE) made of two decameric half-sites that both contain the sequence RRRCWWGYYY.
source: p53 binds to a canonical 20 bp response element (RE) made of two decameric half-sites that both contain the sequence RRRCWWGYYY (R = A/G; W = A/T; Y = C/T).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the p53 response element.

claim: p53 has been shown to bind to decameric half-sites separated by spacers or to single half-sites.
source: p53 has also been shown to bind to decameric half-sites separated by spacers or to single half-sites (Kitayner et al., 2010; Menendez et al., 2013; Vyas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kitayner et al., 2010, Menendez et al., 2013, and Vyas et al., 2017.

claim: SELEX and ChIP analyses yielded p63 binding motifs with high similarity to the p53RE but showed some unique characteristics.
source: Results from systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) (Ortt and Sinha, 2006; Perez et al., 2007) and high-throughput analyses of chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) (Kouwenhoven et al., 2010; McDade et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2006) yielded p63 binding motifs with high similarity to the p53RE but still showed some unique characteristics.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to SELEX and ChIP studies.

claim: The unique characteristics identified for p63REs differed substantially between studies.
source: These unique characteristics identified for p63REs, however, differed substantially between the studies.
evidence: This is an observation about the inconsistency in the literature.

claim: There is limited overlap of p63-dependent genes identified in individual studies.
source: This is in part due to the limited overlap of the p63-dependent genes identified in individual studies (Kouwenhoven et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kouwenhoven et al., 2015b.

claim: 16 publically available gene expression datasets were integrated to generate a specific p63 Expression Score.
source: From 11 genome-wide studies (Abraham et al., 2018; Bao et al., 2015; Carroll et al., 2006; Gallant-Behm et al., 2012; Karsli Uzunbas et al., 2019; Lin-Shiao et al., 2019; Saladi et al., 2017; Somerville et al., 2018; Watanabe et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2012; Zarnegar et al., 2012; Supplementary file 1), 16 publically available gene expression datasets were integrated to generate a specific p63 Expression Score (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.

claim: Genes commonly up-regulated by p63 significantly enrich gene sets associated with cell cycle, epidermis development, and MYC targets.
source: In agreement with the function of p63 as an essential proliferation factor (McDade et al., 2011; Senoo et al., 2007; Truong et al., 2006), epidermal development regulator (Mills et al., 1999; Yang et al., 1999), and MYC network activator (Wu et al., 2012), we find that genes commonly up-regulated by p63 significantly enrich gene sets associated with cell cycle, epidermis development, and MYC targets (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 2A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Genes down-regulated by p63 enrich gene sets connected with interferon response.
source: In line with previous reports (Mehta et al., 2018), genes down-regulated by p63 enrich gene sets connected with interferon response (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 2B and citation to Mehta et al., 2018.

claim: p63 up- and down-regulated genes enrich respective gene sets up- and down-regulated in mammary stem cells.
source: Corroborating the role of p63 in mammary stem cell activity (Chakrabarti et al., 2014) and SCC growth (Ramsey et al., 2013), we find that p63 up- and down-regulated genes enrich respective gene sets up- and down-regulated in mammary stem cells (Figure 2C) and across SCCs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 2C and citation to Chakrabarti et al., 2014.

claim: p63 up- and down-regulated genes enrich respective gene sets up- and down-regulated across SCCs.
source: Corroborating the role of p63 in mammary stem cell activity (Chakrabarti et al., 2014) and SCC growth (Ramsey et al., 2013), we find that p63 up- and down-regulated genes enrich respective gene sets up- and down-regulated in mammary stem cells (Figure 2C) and across SCCs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 2D and citation to Ramsey et al., 2013.

claim: p63 up-regulated genes enrich for mTORC1 signaling genes.
source: In addition to pathways that have been linked to p63 earlier, we find that p63 up-regulated genes enrich for mTORC1 signaling genes and p63 down-regulated genes enrich for gene sets associated with oxidative phosphorylation and aerobic respiration (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: p63 down-regulated genes enrich for gene sets associated with oxidative phosphorylation and aerobic respiration.
source: In addition to pathways that have been linked to p63 earlier, we find that p63 up-regulated genes enrich for mTORC1 signaling genes and p63 down-regulated genes enrich for gene sets associated with oxidative phosphorylation and aerobic respiration (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cell cycle gene regulators (E2F4, E2F6, SIN3A, E2F1, FOXM1, NFYA, and NFYB) are enriched among p63-upregulated genes.
source: In agreement with its established roles, we identify cell cycle gene regulators (E2F4, E2F6, SIN3A, E2F1, FOXM1, NFYA, and NFYB Fischer and Müller, 2017) and the MYC/MAX TFs as being enriched among p63-upregulated genes.
evidence: This is supported by the TF binding enrichment analysis and citation to Fischer and Müller, 2017.

claim: MYC/MAX TFs are enriched among p63-upregulated genes.
source: In agreement with its established roles, we identify cell cycle gene regulators (E2F4, E2F6, SIN3A, E2F1, FOXM1, NFYA, and NFYB Fischer and Müller, 2017) and the MYC/MAX TFs as being enriched among p63-upregulated genes.
evidence: This is supported by the TF binding enrichment analysis.

claim: KLF4 is a potential mediator of p63-dependent gene regulation.
source: Consistent with previous reports, our analysis also identifies KLF4 (Sen et al., 2012) and SMAD4 (Rodriguez Calleja et al., 2016) as potential mediators of p63-dependent gene regulation.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis and citation to Sen et al., 2012.

claim: SMAD4 is a potential mediator of p63-dependent gene regulation.
source: Consistent with previous reports, our analysis also identifies KLF4 (Sen et al., 2012) and SMAD4 (Rodriguez Calleja et al., 2016) as potential mediators of p63-dependent gene regulation.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis and citation to Rodriguez Calleja et al., 2016.

claim: AR, ZMIZ1, SP1, FLI1, and NANOG are novel candidates for mediating the p63-dependent up-regulation of multiple genes.
source: In addition, our analysis reveals that androgen receptor (AR), its co-factor ZMIZ1, as well as SP1, FLI1, and NANOG are novel candidates for mediating the p63-dependent up-regulation of multiple genes.
evidence: This is supported by the TF binding enrichment analysis performed in the study.

claim: SOX2 is a frequent binder of genes down-regulated by p63.
source: Surprisingly, our analysis identified only SOX2 as a frequent binder of genes down-regulated by p63 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the TF binding enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: p63 up-regulated genes enrich DREAM and E2F target genes.
source: Consistent with the strong association of p63 up-regulated genes with the cell cycle (Figure 2A) and with cell cycle regulators (Figure 3A), we find that p63 up-regulated genes enrich DREAM (dimerization partner, RB-like, E2F, and multi-vulval class B) and E2F target genes (Figure 3B), and DREAM target genes appear to be modestly but consistently down-regulated when p63 is lost (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DREAM target genes appear to be modestly but consistently down-regulated when p63 is lost.
source: Consistent with the strong association of p63 up-regulated genes with the cell cycle (Figure 2A) and with cell cycle regulators (Figure 3A), we find that p63 up-regulated genes enrich DREAM (dimerization partner, RB-like, E2F, and multi-vulval class B) and E2F target genes (Figure 3B), and DREAM target genes appear to be modestly but consistently down-regulated when p63 is lost (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Depletion of p63 decreased DREAM target expression without affecting CDKN1A (p21) levels.
source: Strikingly, depletion of p63 decreased their expression even further without affecting CDKN1A (p21) levels (Figure 3D), which indicates a possible cumulative effect that is independent of p53 regulatory functions.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The effect of p63 on DREAM targets is independent of p53 regulatory functions.
source: Strikingly, depletion of p63 decreased their expression even further without affecting CDKN1A (p21) levels (Figure 3D), which indicates a possible cumulative effect that is independent of p53 regulatory functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p21 levels are not affected while DREAM targets are down-regulated.

claim: Negative p53 Expression Scores tend to correlate with positive p63 Expression Scores.
source: In agreement with the up-regulation of cell cycle genes and DREAM targets through p63 (Figures 2A and 3) and their down-regulation through p53 (Fischer et al., 2016a; Fischer et al., 2016b; Schade et al., 2019; Uxa et al., 2019), we noted that negative p53 Expression Scores tend to correlate with positive p63 Expression Scores (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 4A and citations to previous studies.

claim: p53-induced genes appear to be largely unaffected by p63.
source: Furthermore, the results indicate that p53-induced genes (positive p53 Expression Scores) appear to be largely unaffected by p63.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of p53 and p63 Expression Scores.

claim: Expression data for 343 target genes with strong evidence for direct up-regulation by p53 do not show consistent expression changes upon knockdown or induction of p63.
source: Consistently, expression data for 343 target genes with strong evidence for direct up-regulation by p53 (Fischer, 2017), do not show consistent expression changes upon knockdown or induction of p63 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 4B and citation to Fischer, 2017.

claim: Basal expression of the majority of p53 target genes is not affected by p63.
source: Together, these results indicate that basal expression of the majority of p53 target genes is not affected by p63.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of p53 target gene expression in p63 perturbation experiments.

claim: More than half of the p63 peaks are present in two or more datasets.
source: Notably, p63 and p53 data was collected from cells with strong basal p63 expression and stimulated p53 expression, respectively. While the majority of all p53 ChIP-seq peaks occurs in only one of the experiments, more than half of the p63 peaks are present in two or more datasets (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The number of identified p63 binding sites was higher than p53 binding sites despite integrating more p53 datasets.
source: Even though we were able to integrate substantially more p53 datasets, the number of identified p63 binding sites was still higher (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: p63 occupies many more binding sites as compared to p53.
source: This indicates that p63 occupies many more binding sites as compared to p53.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p63 has more binding sites despite fewer datasets.

claim: When more datasets agree on p53- and p63-binding sites, these sequences are more likely to harbor a canonical p53 and p63RE.
source: Importantly, when more datasets agree on p53- and p63-binding sites, these sequences are more likely to harbor a canonical p53 and p63RE, facilitating the motif discovery by tools such as HOMER (Heinz et al., 2010) and enriching bona fide binding sites (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 5D and citation to Heinz et al., 2010.

claim: p63-binding sites display a highly conserved C, G, C, and G at positions 4, 7, 14, and 17, respectively.
source: Comparison of the primary 'p53+p63', 'p53', and 'p63' motifs suggests that p63-binding sites display a highly conserved C, G, C, and G at positions 4, 7, 14, and 17, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The second round of motif search revealed a p53RE containing a 1 bp spacer.
source: The second round revealed a p53RE containing a 1 bp spacer (p53 secondary motif), supporting the model that p53 can bind to spacer-containing p53REs (Vyas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis and citation to Vyas et al., 2017.

claim: p53 can bind to a single half-site.
source: The results further indicate that p53 can bind to a single half-site (p53 tertiary motif) and that this single half-site is more constrained at positions 5 and 6 as well as the flanking regions than half-sites in the canonical p53RE (e.g. primary p53+p63 and p53 motifs).
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Sole half-sites together with spacer-containing p53REs underlie only ~5% of p53-bound sites.
source: Sole half-sites together with spacer-containing p53REs underlie only ~5% of p53-bound sites (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: p53 and p63 appear to be able to bind to three-quarter sites.
source: Furthermore, p53 and p63 appear to be able to bind to three-quarter sites (secondary and quaternary p53+p63 and p63 motifs), while p63 can generally bind to a broader spectrum of sequences as compared to p53 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: p63 can generally bind to a broader spectrum of sequences as compared to p53.
source: Furthermore, p53 and p63 appear to be able to bind to three-quarter sites (secondary and quaternary p53+p63 and p63 motifs), while p63 can generally bind to a broader spectrum of sequences as compared to p53 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The broader binding repertoire likely underlies p63's capacity to engage with substantially more binding sites than does p53.
source: This broader binding repertoire likely underlies p63's capacity to engage with substantially more binding sites than does p53.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p63 binds more diverse sequences and has more binding sites.

claim: The vast majority (~70%) of p53- and p63-binding sites harbor full-length p53 and p63REs.
source: It is important to note that the vast majority (~70%) of p53- and p63-binding sites harbor full-length p53 and p63REs (Figures 6 and 7, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: There is a good correlation between p53- and p63-binding site occupation.
source: There is a good correlation between p53- and p63-binding site occupation, and most sites commonly bound by p53 are also frequently bound by p63 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: p63 binds many sites that are not bound by p53.
source: However, p63 binds many sites that are not bound by p53 (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: p53 binding is strongly constrained to canonical p53RE.
source: More importantly, p53 binding is strongly constrained to canonical p53RE (Figure 5—figure supplements 1C–D and 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1C–D and 2A–C.

claim: p63 binding appears not to benefit from a more canonical p63RE.
source: In contrast, p63 binding appears not to benefit from a more canonical p63RE (Figure 5—figure supplements 1E–F and 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1E–F and 2D–F.

claim: Sequence-specific binding is particularly important to recruit p53.
source: These data suggest that sequence-specific binding is particularly important to recruit p53, while p63 only requires minimal sequence identity and could require additional co-factors to bind and ultimately regulate its target genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p53 binding strongly correlates with canonical motifs while p63 does not.

claim: p63 only requires minimal sequence identity and could require additional co-factors to bind and ultimately regulate its target genes.
source: These data suggest that sequence-specific binding is particularly important to recruit p53, while p63 only requires minimal sequence identity and could require additional co-factors to bind and ultimately regulate its target genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p63 binding does not strongly correlate with canonical motifs.

claim: No additional motif was substantially enriched in the vicinity of 'p53' or 'p53+p63' binding sites.
source: Consistent with earlier analyses (Verfaillie et al., 2016), no additional motif was substantially enriched in the vicinity of 'p53' or 'p53+p63' binding sites.
evidence: This is supported by the motif search analysis and citation to Verfaillie et al., 2016.

claim: Unique p63-binding sites were consistently enriched for AP-1 (bZIP) in addition to bHLH motifs.
source: Consistent with the co-enrichment of AP-1 and p63 at enhancers (Lin-Shiao et al., 2018), we found that unique p63-binding sites were consistently enriched for AP-1 (bZIP) in addition to bHLH motifs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and citation to Lin-Shiao et al., 2018.

claim: p300, MAF, SOX2, BANF1, and KMT2D are potential co-binders of p63.
source: In agreement with earlier studies, the analysis identified p300 (Katoh et al., 2019), MAF (Lopez-Pajares et al., 2015), SOX2 (Watanabe et al., 2014), BANF1 (also known as BAF) (Bao et al., 2015), and KMT2D (Lin-Shiao et al., 2018) as potential co-binders of p63; as well as TRIM28 (Doyle et al., 2010), BRD4 (Stewart et al., 2013), p300 (Lill et al., 1997), ZBTB33 (KAISO) (Koh et al., 2014), CDK9 (Claudio et al., 2006), and HEXIM1 (Lew et al., 2012) as potential co-binders of p53.
evidence: This is supported by the CistromeDB analysis and multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: TRIM28, BRD4, p300, ZBTB33 (KAISO), CDK9, and HEXIM1 are potential co-binders of p53.
source: In agreement with earlier studies, the analysis identified p300 (Katoh et al., 2019), MAF (Lopez-Pajares et al., 2015), SOX2 (Watanabe et al., 2014), BANF1 (also known as BAF) (Bao et al., 2015), and KMT2D (Lin-Shiao et al., 2018) as potential co-binders of p63; as well as TRIM28 (Doyle et al., 2010), BRD4 (Stewart et al., 2013), p300 (Lill et al., 1997), ZBTB33 (KAISO) (Koh et al., 2014), CDK9 (Claudio et al., 2006), and HEXIM1 (Lew et al., 2012) as potential co-binders of p53.
evidence: This is supported by the CistromeDB analysis and multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: KDM1A, PRMT1, and GRHL2 are potential co-binders of p63 that have not been identified before.
source: Moreover, our analysis identified potential co-binders that to our knowledge have not been identified before, such as KDM1A, PRMT1, and GRHL2 for p63 and BRD9, ZNF131, and C17orf49 for p53.
evidence: This is supported by the CistromeDB analysis performed in the study.

claim: BRD9, ZNF131, and C17orf49 are potential co-binders of p53 that have not been identified before.
source: Moreover, our analysis identified potential co-binders that to our knowledge have not been identified before, such as KDM1A, PRMT1, and GRHL2 for p63 and BRD9, ZNF131, and C17orf49 for p53.
evidence: This is supported by the CistromeDB analysis performed in the study.

claim: The new potential co-binders may contribute to shaping the DNA-binding landscapes that are specific to p63 and p53.
source: Importantly, these new potential co-binders appear to be unique to either p63 or p53, suggesting that they may contribute to shaping the DNA-binding landscapes that are specific to p63 and p53 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these co-binders are unique to either p63 or p53.

claim: 138 genes were identified as high-probability candidates as directly up-regulated by p63.
source: Using these thresholds we identified 138 and 42 high-probability candidates as directly up- and down-regulated by p63, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the integration of binding data, expression data, and enhancer:gene associations.

claim: 42 genes were identified as high-probability candidates as directly down-regulated by p63.
source: Using these thresholds we identified 138 and 42 high-probability candidates as directly up- and down-regulated by p63, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the integration of binding data, expression data, and enhancer:gene associations.

claim: The 180 genes that passed conservative filtering contain many genes that are known direct p63 targets.
source: The 180 (138 up-regulated and 42 down-regulated) genes that passed our conservative filtering contain many genes that are known direct p63 targets, such as RAB38 (Barton et al., 2010), S100A2 (Kirschner et al., 2008; Lapi et al., 2006), HAS3 (Compagnone et al., 2017), IRF6 (Thomason et al., 2010), PTHLH (Somerville et al., 2018), GPX2 (Yan and Chen, 2006), JAG1 (Sasaki et al., 2002), MMP14 (Lodillinsky et al., 2016), NRG1 (Forster et al., 2014), and PLAC8 (Gallant-Behm et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies identifying these as p63 targets.

claim: The integration of enhancer:gene associations enabled the identification of genes that are likely regulated by p63 through enhancers.
source: Importantly, the integration of enhancer:gene associations enabled the identification of genes that are likely regulated by p63 through enhancers, such as IL1B, MREG, MYO5A, RRP12, SNCA, AK4, and EHD4 (Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the methodology and results shown in Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Out of the 180 high-probability p63 target genes, 32 are also commonly up- or down-regulated in SCCs compared to non-SCC cancers.
source: Out of the 180 high-probability p63 target genes 32 (28 up- and four down-regulated) are also identified as being commonly up- or down-regulated in SCCs compared to non-SCC cancers (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2018; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison with TCGA data and citation to Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2018.

claim: Several genes commonly up-regulated by p63 and in SCC have been identified to promote SCC growth or invasion.
source: Importantly, several of the genes commonly up-regulated by p63 as well as in SCC have been identified to promote SCC growth or invasion, such as LAD1 (Abe et al., 2019), TMEM40 (Zhang et al., 2019), FGFBP1 (Czubayko et al., 1997), IL1B (Lee et al., 2015), FAT2 (Dang et al., 2016), FOSL1 (Usui et al., 2012), LPAR3 (Brusevold et al., 2014), MMP14 (Pang et al., 2016), and RASSF6 (Zheng et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Expression levels of the 28-gene set correlate significantly negatively with HNSC patient survival.
source: We find that expression levels of our gene set indeed correlate significantly negatively with HNSC patient survival (COX likelihood ratio test p=0.032).
evidence: This is supported by the survival analysis of TCGA HNSC patient data.

claim: The sample group with low expression of the 28-gene set had the most favorable prognosis.
source: While the sample group with low expression had the most favorable prognosis, the null hypothesis could not be rejected in the direct comparison with patients with high average expression levels (p=0.090; Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by the survival analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Upon contrasting the low-expression group with all remaining samples, a significant improvement of survival was detected.
source: However, upon contrasting the low-expression group with all remaining samples, a significant improvement of survival was detected (p=0.024; Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the survival analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Expression of the 28-gene set correlated positively with p63 expression when p63 expression was rather low (FPKM <20).
source: Expression of the 28-gene set correlated positively with p63 expression when p63 expression was rather low (FPKM <20), but showed a saturation and no further correlation when p63 expression was high (FPKM >20; Figure 8C and D, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: p63 levels influence the 28-gene set in a switch-like manner where a saturation of p63-dependent activation is quickly reached in HNSC cells.
source: This indicates that p63 levels influence the 28-gene set in a switch-like manner where a saturation of p63-dependent activation is quickly reached in HNSC cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the 28-gene set shows saturation at high p63 levels.

claim: The genes commonly up-regulated by p63 and in SCC influence the prognosis of HNSC patients.
source: Together, these findings indicate that the genes commonly up-regulated by p63 and in SCC influence the prognosis of HNSC patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival analysis results.

claim: Many p63 target genes initially described in mouse could not be confirmed to be p63-regulated in human.
source: Because p63 target genes, very much like p53 target genes (Fischer, 2020; Fischer, 2019), differ substantially between mouse and human (Sethi et al., 2017), many p63 target genes initially described in mouse could not be confirmed to be p63-regulated in this study using human data.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fischer, 2020, Fischer, 2019, and Sethi et al., 2017.

claim: p63-binding sites are frequently associated with enhancer regions and enhancer identity.
source: Given that p63-binding sites are frequently associated with enhancer regions and enhancer identity, we have integrated enhancer:gene associations to identify target genes that are regulated by p63 through direct binding to associated enhancers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p63 binding patterns.

claim: Most sites bound by p53 are also commonly occupied by p63.
source: Most importantly, our results could explain why a substantial fraction of DNA sites is occupied exclusively by p53 or p63. While most sites bound by p53 are also commonly occupied by p63 (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), single half-sites and half-sites separated by spacers underlie many sites that are only bound by p53 (Figures 5F and 6), supporting earlier findings whereby p53 can be recruited through spacer-containing motifs (Vyas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Single half-sites and half-sites separated by spacers underlie many sites that are only bound by p53.
source: While most sites bound by p53 are also commonly occupied by p63 (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), single half-sites and half-sites separated by spacers underlie many sites that are only bound by p53 (Figures 5F and 6), supporting earlier findings whereby p53 can be recruited through spacer-containing motifs (Vyas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis shown in Figures 5F and 6 and citation to Vyas et al., 2017.

claim: Only 1.1% to 5.1% of the p53 peaks contain p53REs with 1 bp spacers or half sites that are possibly separated by longer spacers.
source: However, while spacers reportedly have been identified in fifty percent of 200 analyzed p53REs (Vyas et al., 2017), our genome-wide quantification of motifs underlying 7705 high confidence p53 peaks based on an unbiased motif search using HOMER revealed that only 1.1% to 5.1% of the p53 peaks contain p53REs with 1 bp spacers or half sites that are possibly separated by longer spacers (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6 and citation to Vyas et al., 2017.

claim: Relying on the CWWG core motif and the flanking regions may enable p53 to bind to spacer-containing sites.
source: Mechanistically, our results imply that relying on the CWWG core motif and the flanking regions may enable p53 to bind to those sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the motif analysis results.

claim: The two CNNG core motifs underlie p63, but not p53REs.
source: In contrast, the two CNNG core motifs that underlie p63, but not p53REs, offer an explanation why a substantial fraction of DNA sites is bound exclusively by p63 (Figures 5F and 7), supporting one of the models established earlier (McDade et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis shown in Figures 5F and 7 and citation to McDade et al., 2014.

claim: p63's ability to bind to a greater variety of recognition motifs likely underlies the markedly greater number of p63 compared to p53-binding sites in the genome.
source: Notably, p63's ability to bind to a greater variety of recognition motifs likely underlies the markedly greater number of p63 compared to p53-binding sites in the genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p63 binds more diverse motifs and has more binding sites.

claim: Factors bound to AP-1 (bZIP) and bHLH motifs may specifically support p63 binding.
source: In addition, our motif search indicates that factors bound to AP-1 (bZIP) and bHLH motifs may specifically support p63 binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), and transcription factor enrichment analysis identified the bZIP TF MAF, the TF GRHL2, the chromatin remodeler BANF1, the histone methyltransferase PRMT1, and the ZNF750/KDM1A/KLF4 complex, which was previously shown to operate downstream of p63 (Boxer et al., 2014), as potential co-binders that could help to facilitate p63 binding to certain genomic loci (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ZNF750/KDM1A/KLF4 complex was previously shown to operate downstream of p63.
source: In addition, our motif search indicates that factors bound to AP-1 (bZIP) and bHLH motifs may specifically support p63 binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), and transcription factor enrichment analysis identified the bZIP TF MAF, the TF GRHL2, the chromatin remodeler BANF1, the histone methyltransferase PRMT1, and the ZNF750/KDM1A/KLF4 complex, which was previously shown to operate downstream of p63 (Boxer et al., 2014), as potential co-binders that could help to facilitate p63 binding to certain genomic loci (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boxer et al., 2014.

claim: p63 could enable the binding of co-factor TFs to respective loci given its pioneer role.
source: Considering its pioneer role, p63 could vice versa enable the binding of these TFs to the respective loci.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential role of p63 as a pioneer factor.

claim: p63 and p73 form stable heterotetramers.
source: Given that p63 and p73 form stable heterotetramers (Gebel et al., 2016), p73 may possess binding specificities that are highly similar to those identified for p63.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gebel et al., 2016.

claim: p73 may possess binding specificities that are highly similar to those identified for p63.
source: Given that p63 and p73 form stable heterotetramers (Gebel et al., 2016), p73 may possess binding specificities that are highly similar to those identified for p63.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p63 and p73 form heterotetramers.

claim: The iterative de novo search algorithm enabled the identification of spacer-containing p53REs.
source: Our iterative de novo search algorithm enabled the identification of spacer-containing p53REs, indicating that our approach uncovers second-tier TF binding motifs invisible to standard approaches.
evidence: This is supported by the methodology and results of the motif analysis.

claim: p63 is more frequently involved in a direct up-regulation as opposed to a direct down-regulation of target genes.
source: Consistent with results from an earlier genome-wide study (Yang et al., 2006), our findings imply that p63 is more frequently involved in a direct up-regulation as opposed to a direct down-regulation of target genes (Figure 3A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis and citation to Yang et al., 2006.

claim: p63 up-regulates target genes through its alternative TAD located at the N-terminus.
source: Mechanistically, p63 has been shown to up-regulate target genes through its alternative TAD located at the N-terminus while the C-terminus is important for down-regulation (Helton et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Helton et al., 2006.

claim: The C-terminus of p63 is important for down-regulation of target genes.
source: Mechanistically, p63 has been shown to up-regulate target genes through its alternative TAD located at the N-terminus while the C-terminus is important for down-regulation (Helton et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Helton et al., 2006.

claim: Exogenous expression of different isoforms of p53 family members and their antagonistic effects on target gene promoters suggested a model whereby p63 exhibits a dominant negative effect on other p53 family members.
source: Exogenous expression of different isoforms of p53 family members and their antagonistic effects on target gene promoters in luciferase reporter assays suggested a model whereby p63 exhibits a dominant negative effect on other p53 family members (Mundt et al., 2010; Westfall et al., 2003; Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mundt et al., 2010, Westfall et al., 2003, and Yang et al., 1998.

claim: Genome-wide studies showed that the groups of p63-regulated genes and p53-regulated genes show only very little overlap.
source: Inconsistent with its reputation as dominant negative regulator of p53, however, genome-wide studies showed that the groups of p63-regulated genes and p53-regulated genes show only very little overlap (Gallant-Behm et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gallant-Behm et al., 2012.

claim: p63 is more likely to support than to inhibit p53 activity.
source: A recent analysis of DNA sites bound and of genes regulated by p53 and p63 revealed that p63 is more likely to support than to inhibit p53 activity (Karsli Uzunbas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Karsli Uzunbas et al., 2019.

claim: p63 does not commonly interfere with target gene up-regulation by p53 but except for cell cycle genes they regulate largely distinct gene sets.
source: Our analysis further supports the notion that p63 does not commonly interfere with target gene up-regulation by p53 but that except for cell cycle genes they regulate largely distinct gene sets (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: AR, ZMIZ1, SP1, FLI1, and NANOG are novel candidate nodes in the p63 GRN.
source: In addition to known mediators of p63-dependent gene regulation, such as MYC and KLF4, we identify AR and its co-factor ZMIZ1, SP1, FLI1, and NANOG as novel candidate nodes in the p63 GRN (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the TF enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cell cycle genes are antagonistically regulated by p53 and p63.
source: In agreement with the tumor suppressor role of p53 and the oncogenic role of p63, we find that cell cycle genes are antagonistically regulated by p53 and p63 (Figures 2A and 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figures 2A and 4A.

claim: Cell cycle genes are down-regulated by p53 indirectly through p21 and the cell cycle repressor complexes DREAM and RB-E2F.
source: On the one hand, cell cycle genes are well-known to be down-regulated by p53 indirectly through the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21 and the cell cycle repressor complexes DREAM and RB-E2F (Fischer et al., 2016a; Fischer et al., 2016b; Schade et al., 2019; Uxa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Cell cycle genes are down-regulated upon loss of p63 through regulating p21 signaling and the DREAM component p130.
source: On the other hand, cell cycle genes are down-regulated upon loss of p63 and this p63-dependent regulation reportedly occurs through regulating p21 signaling and the DREAM component p130 (McDade et al., 2011; Truong et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McDade et al., 2011 and Truong et al., 2006.

claim: Multiple cell cycle genes were predicted as direct p63 targets.
source: In addition to indirect effects, we also predicted multiple cell cycle genes as direct p63 targets (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the target gene prediction shown in Table 1.

claim: A loss of p63 may substantially contribute to the effect of p53 in reducing cell cycle gene expression.
source: Consequently, a loss of p63 may substantially contribute to the effect of p53 in reducing cell cycle gene expression (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p63 loss affects DREAM targets independently of p21.

claim: The entire set of cell cycle genes may be subsequently up-regulated indirectly through p63's pro-proliferative targets.
source: In addition of p63's role in driving the expression of some cell cycle genes, the entire set of cell cycle genes may be subsequently up-regulated indirectly through p63's pro-proliferative targets.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about indirect effects of p63 on cell cycle genes.

claim: The up-regulation of cell cycle genes occurs in most cancers.
source: While the up-regulation of cell cycle genes occurs in most cancers (Whitfield et al., 2006), we find that p63 additionally regulates genes that are specifically altered across SCCs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Whitfield et al., 2006.

claim: p63 additionally regulates genes that are specifically altered across SCCs.
source: While the up-regulation of cell cycle genes occurs in most cancers (Whitfield et al., 2006), we find that p63 additionally regulates genes that are specifically altered across SCCs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: p63 and its target genes play a critical role in determining the transcriptional profile of SCC.
source: These results underscore the critical role of p63 and its target genes in determining the transcriptional profile of SCC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p63 regulates genes specifically altered in SCCs.

claim: NRG1 is a p63 target in SCC that can be inhibited to block SCC proliferation and tumor growth.
source: An example of a p63 target in SCC is NRG1, which can be inhibited to block SCC proliferation and tumor growth (Hegde et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hegde et al., 2019.

claim: The 28-gene set may contain particularly promising candidates for therapeutic interventions and for the use as biomarkers.
source: Thus, this 28-gene set may contain particularly promising candidates for therapeutic interventions and for the use as biomarkers.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the 28-gene set correlates with patient survival.
